title: Accessibility Audit — break it, audit it, fix it
description: Bramblewick Goods, a fictional candle shop, ships with twelve deliberate WCAG 2.2 failures: a missing alt, low-contrast prices, an unlabelled email field, a clickable div, a removed focus outline, a skipped heading level, no skip link, a keyboard trap in the quick-view modal, an error shown only in red, an autoplaying banner with no pause or reduced-motion support, 16 px quantity buttons and a Spanish phrase without lang. Each has a fix toggle, and twelve in-page checks update live: computed contrast ratios, measured target sizes with the 24 px spacing test, a behaviour probe of the modal, CSS rule inspection for focus and reduced motion. Every result cites its success criterion by number, name and level, and the audit exports as Markdown.
prompt: Build an accessibility audit demo. Render a fictional sample site (a small shop page) inside the page with about 12 deliberate, realistic WCAG 2.2 failures: missing alt, low contrast, unlabeled input, div-button, focus not visible, skipped heading level, no skip link, a keyboard trap in a modal, a color-only error state, autoplaying motion without reduced-motion support, target size too small, and missing lang on a fragment. Give each issue a toggle to fix it individually, with an audit panel that runs in-page checks and updates live. Cite success criteria correctly, number + name + level (e.g. 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) AA, 2.4.7 Focus Visible AA, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) AA, new in 2.2), and verify each number and level. Provide an exportable audit report in Markdown, and a CTA to Services that mentions an a11y audit via hourly. The broken site must not break the page-level smoke contract: scope it inside the page so there's no horizontal scroll, and no real keyboard trap for the test user outside a demo modal that is clearly escapable through a visible 'exit demo' control. The spec should check that each issue is detected when broken and cleared when fixed (compute contrast ratios with the WCAG formula in the test), the report text, and keyboard access to the toggles.

methodology: One flip at a time: from the all-broken state, each of the twelve toggles is switched on alone. Exactly that check must turn to pass while the other eleven stay failed, and switching it off must bring the failure back.

Contrast with the spec's own formula: WCAG relative luminance and contrast are implemented in the test and checked against published values (21:1 for black on white, 4.54:1 for #767676, 4.48:1 for #777777). They are then applied to the browser's computed colours. The broken price is under 4.5:1 and the page's reported ratio matches to two decimals. After the fix, every visible text node in the sample passes the test's own scan.

Measured, not assumed: quantity buttons are measured with boundingBox, 16 by 16 and 18 px apart when broken, so the 24 px spacing exception can't apply, and at least 24 by 24 when fixed. Focus visibility is read from the computed outline of a link focused with the Tab key.

Behaviour, not markup alone: the keyboard trap is exercised with real Tab, Shift+Tab and Escape presses, the harness Exit button must be reachable and return focus to the opener, and reduced motion is emulated with emulateMedia to show the banner ignores it until fixed.

Citations and report: the expected success criteria for all twelve issues are written in the spec from the WCAG 2.2 recommendation and must match the chips exactly. The downloaded Markdown must contain every criterion, one table row and one fix per failing issue, and a result line that tracks the live state.
risks: Twelve checks are not an audit tool. They target the failures planted here, and the page states they are not Lighthouse, axe or a conformance claim.
The language-of-parts check is a small word-list heuristic for Spanish, not language detection.
The keyboard-trap check probes the modal by opening it without moving focus and sending a synthetic Escape. It knows this modal's pattern, not every possible trap.
The skipped-heading finding is filed under 1.3.1 as advisory, since skipping levels is a best-practice issue more than a hard failure. The page labels it that way.
qa.playwright: Accessibility-aware locators did most of the verification: getByRole with a name or heading level, toHaveAccessibleName and toHaveAccessibleDescription confirm each fix changes what assistive tech sees, not just a class name. emulateMedia({ reducedMotion }) and element.getAnimations() made the motion check concrete, and boundingBox gave independent target measurements. Keyboard work (Tab, Shift+Tab, Escape, Space on role=switch toggles) runs on desktop only, since the mobile project emulates a touch phone. The spec passed on its first full run, so I can't claim it caught a page bug. The one change afterwards was the spec's own: I replaced a lenient comparison of the report preview with an exact one.
coverage: All 12 issues detected on load, with exact success criterion citations
Each fix clears only its own check; re-breaking restores it
Contrast via the WCAG formula, verified against reference values
Target size measured, with the spacing exception
Keyboard trap, harness exit and Escape after the fix
Focus outline, reduced motion and the pause control
Accessible names, roles, heading levels, lang, alt, error description, skip link
Markdown report text, toggles by keyboard, honesty note and CTA

a11y: The page practises what it audits: the fix toggles are labelled role=switch checkboxes, the score is a polite live region, pass and fail are written in words, and every citation is text. The broken sample is contained. It clips its own overflow, its failures are scoped to its own classes, and its modal, though a deliberate trap until fixed, always contains a visible, striped Exit demo button that closes it and returns focus.
